threat: An unauthenticated local process reaches a state-changing management route (e.g. /v1/runtime install/start) and changes machine state.
strengths: The gateway does have a centralized management gate at the single dispatch point in Kernel/API/src/server.ts (handleRequest, ~L441-448): '/v1/runtime' is explicitly in MANAGEMENT_PREFIXES (L406), so POST /v1/runtime/opencode/install and /start are covered and are not protected per-handler-by-omission. Kernel/API/test/admin-gate.test.js explicitly lists both runtime routes in its MANAGEMENT array (L66-69) and asserts a bare request (no Origin, no Authorization) gets 401 when enforcement is on (L73-81). A structural guard (same file, L120-164) cross-checks the router's served paths against the prefix list so a future route - including one that names a constant like runtimePrefix - cannot silently sit outside the gate (the comment records that this exact family was ungated for months). Defense in depth at the HTTP layer: loopback-only bind plus a Host-header check returning 421 (server.ts L139-146, L189-192) defeating DNS rebinding; CORS origin allowlist and cross-site request checks returning 403 (L193-206); a 415 content-type check (L251-254); no-store headers on management paths (L221); rate limiting on the LLM surface. A per-launch 256-bit dashboard token (core/dashboard-token.ts) uses constant-time comparison, is published only after a successful bind, is regenerated every start and stored 0600, and the shipped CLI proxy forwards it only for sec-fetch-site: same-origin requests (cli/server-src/static.mjs L151-155). API keys are random, SHA-256 hashed, one-time revealed and compared in constant time. Errors to non-dashboard callers are sanitized via sendError(..., isTrustedDashboard(auth)) (server.ts L256).
weaknesses: The gate is conditional, not absolute: ApiKeyManager.authorize() returns early whenever enforcement is off or no store is configured (core/api-key-manager.ts L148-150), and admin-gate.test.js L101-108 deliberately asserts that with enforcement off the whole management surface - including /v1/runtime/opencode/install and /start - stays open to a bare local request ('the documented local mode'). In that configuration the threat is fully realized: opencode-runtime.ts install()/start() download a network artifact, chmod/write an executable into the data dir, write config/pid files (0600) and spawn a long-lived 'opencode serve --service' process, so an unauthenticated local process changes real machine state. Even with enforcement on, the in-scope actor (a same-user local process - SECURITY.md L30-32 states this is the threat model) can read the 0600 dashboard-token file (same UID) and set any allowlisted Origin (defaults include http://localhost:5173 etc., core/http.ts L21), making auth.kind='dashboard' (server.ts L211-218) and skipping the gate entirely; SECURITY.md L65-68 concedes a local process can obtain the token, and L157-159 lists Origin-based dashboard trust as an accepted limitation. There is no route-level authorization: AuthContext carries no scopes/roles (core/runtime.ts L79-93) and any key that passes the gate can reach install/start. The OAuth callback carve-out (server.ts L203, L441) is a further unauthenticated path and the preflight OPTIONS is answered before auth (SECURITY.md L166). Install integrity is only recorded (SHA) not verified because upstream publishes no checksum (SECURITY.md L162-164). Net: strong against browser/CSRF/DNS-rebinding vectors, but the specific local-process threat is achievable in the documented local mode and bypassable via token-file read, which is exactly the actor the policy says is in scope.

threat: A browser page on another origin obtains the dashboard token or makes the gateway trust it as the dashboard.
strengths: A per-launch 256-bit dashboard token is minted on every start, published only after the port is bound, stored 0600 in a 0700 state directory, compared in constant time, and regenerated on restart (Kernel/API/src/core/dashboard-token.ts, Kernel/API/test/dashboard-token.test.js, Kernel/API/test/dashboard-token-bind-order.test.js). The browser never holds it: both the Vite dev proxy and the shipped CLI static proxy read the file server-side and attach the token only when the browser marks the request sec-fetch-site: same-origin, with the shipped proxy also stripping any caller-supplied Origin and token header before deciding (vite.config.ts, cli/server-src/static.mjs). The gateway grants auth.kind='dashboard' only when the request has an exact allowlisted Origin AND a matching token; management paths not so trusted fall through to the API-key gate (Kernel/API/src/server.ts L193-218, L441-448). A loopback-only bind plus a Host-header check returning 421 defeats DNS rebinding; non-allowlisted Origins get 403, wildcard CORS is refused, and cross-site requests are refused except exact OAuth callback navigations (Kernel/API/src/core/http.ts, core/url.ts, core/config.ts). Targeted tests pin that an allowlisted Origin without the token gets 401, that a cross-site page through the shipped proxy does not get a 200, that a rebinding Host gets 421, and that the served shell points the browser at its own origin (tests/cli-dashboard-proxy.test.js, Kernel/API/test/server.test.js). Browser storage is restricted by test to two non-credential keys with sessionStorage, cookies, IndexedDB and the Cache API at zero, and no renderer module references credential material (tests/browser-storage.test.js, tests/desktop-ipc.test.js).
weaknesses: The token is optional at the createGatewayServer boundary: when an embedder omits options.dashboardToken, tokenOk is unconditionally true and Origin alone decides dashboard trust (server.ts L213-215). startGatewayServer always supplies one and a structural test asserts that, but the weaker branch is reachable by direct embedders, and SECURITY.md records Origin-based trust as an accepted limitation. The proxy's trust signal is sec-fetch-site, a browser-set hint rather than a cryptographic proof: a same-user local process can forge it against the loopback dev proxy and receive the token, which the docs concede. The dev proxy also copies every caller header except host and only overwrites the token header on a same-origin request, so a cross-origin caller that already knew the token could forward it (CORS and the gateway's Origin allowlist still constrain this, so it is defence in depth rather than a live bypass). The default CORS allowlist is broad - 5173, 5174, 20137, 20138 on both loopback names plus https://localhost and http://localhost - so any local service on one of those origins is an acceptable origin, though still tokenless. The cross-origin tests drive raw HTTP with hand-set headers rather than a real browser page, so the browser's forbidden-header enforcement is assumed rather than exercised. SECURITY.md L62-64 still says the token protects only the dev dashboard and that a production build has no proxy, which is stale since the shipped CLI server began proxying in 3.74.1; that drift could mislead a reviewer about the real boundary. Net: against the stated actor (a web page on another origin with no local code execution) I found no path to the token or to dashboard trust; the residuals are boundary/configuration assumptions and embedder ergonomics, not an exploitable browser-origin flaw.

threat: A provider-supplied endpoint or a stored connection causes a server-side request to a private/internal destination (SSRF).
strengths: There is a real, centralized, defense-in-depth SSRF design rather than a single check. The URL guard (Kernel/API/src/core/url.ts) enforces HTTPS for every remote provider URL and allows cleartext http: only to loopback hostnames; it rejects userinfo, blocks private IP text at save time and again on every request via isPrivateHostname() (a broad list: 0/8, 10/8, 127/8, 172.16-31, 192.168, 192.0.0/24 incl. the 192.0.0.192 metadata host, 169.254/16, 100.64/10 CGNAT, 198.18-19, 224/4+, plus .local/.internal, IPv6 fc/fd/fe80-fe bf, ::1 and ::), and handles the non-obvious bypasses: a trailing DNS dot, decimal/hex IP spellings normalized by the WHATWG URL parser, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 (https://[::ffff:169.254.169.254] normalizes to [::ffff:a9fe:a9fe] and is unwrapped to 169.254.169.254 and refused). resolveProviderUrl() guards base-path escape and forbids scheme-relative/backslash paths; sanitizeProviderHeaders() blocks credential, CRLF and transport (Host, Content-Length, etc.) headers, and the transport uses redirect:'error' so an open-redirect cannot be used to pivot. Crucially, the gateway adds a request-time DNS check: FetchHttpTransport.request() and .stream() both call assertSafeProviderRequestUrl() and then await checkDestination via assertPublicDestination (Kernel/API/src/core/destination-check.ts), which resolves the host (bounded 2.5s system lookup, deduplicated in-flight, 60s verdict cache), judges every returned address, refuses on any private answer, and refuses names that do not resolve. That check is wired into both transports the gateway builds (the static registry in core/config.ts and the on-demand/generic resolver transport in core/service.ts), so a stored custom endpoint - including the synthesized OpenAICompatibleAdapter built for an unregistered provider in core/provider-resolver.ts - goes through it, and the SDK OpenAI-compatible adapter performs model discovery (/models) through the injected transport too (Kernel/SDK/openai/lib/openai-compatible.ts), not a raw fetch. Stored connections are re-validated on load and backup restore (normalizeInput -> assertSafeProviderRequestUrl), and at request time regardless. All other server-side fetches in routes go to fixed first-party URLs (DuckDuckGo search, GitHub releases, ChatGPT first-party origin guard in chatgptFirstParty.ts, OpenCode Console, ZCode OAuth), and message image_url values are only text-checked and forwarded to the provider, not downloaded locally. Tests are strong and measured against real listeners: private-destinations.test.js pins the full range list and the IPv4-mapped metadata case, destination-check.test.js runs a local stub DNS to prove nip.io->loopback is refused, a public answer allowed, a non-resolving name refused, cache on/off behavior, and that the user-facing error names the private-address cause; transport.test.js-style assertions cover the guard, and SECURITY.md / docs/SPEC-SDK.md document the boundary explicitly.
weaknesses: The central residual is the one the code itself documents and does not fix: check/connect are two separate DNS resolutions. assertPublicDestination() validates one lookup, then global fetch resolves the host again on connect; an authoritative DNS for a provider-supplied endpoint that answers public to the check and private to the connection wins the race, so a stored https://attacker-controlled.example endpoint can be rebound to loopback/an internal address (the 60s verdict cache widens the window). Closing it needs a connect-time/pinned-IP policy that Node's global fetch does not expose; SECURITY.md:153-156 records this as an accepted limitation and docs/SPEC-SDK.md:93 still describes the older text-only state. Related to this, resolveForDestinationCheck()'s public-rescue discards a private system answer whenever the system set is all-private (systemIsAllPrivate ? published : [...]), contradicting its own 'refuse on any private answer' rule: a hostname remapped to a private IP locally (/etc/hosts or local DNS) but public on 8.8.8.8 is judged public and allowed, while the actual fetch still uses the local resolver and connects to the private IP. The cleartext exemption is broad by design: isLoopbackHostname() accepts all of 127.0.0.0/8 and ::1, and a stored connection may point http:// at any loopback port (Ollama is the intended case), so the gateway will perform server-side requests to arbitrary loopback services. The private-literal check is text/prefix based and misses IPv6 transition prefixes that embed IPv4 (6to4 2002::/16, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, Teredo), and only .local/.internal are suffix-blocked rather than a fuller internal-name list; in practice the request-time DNS check catches most of these once resolved, but it does not catch loopback (exempt) or a successful rebind. checkDestination is optional on the SDK FetchHttpTransport and defaults to absent, so any embedder that constructs its own transport (or an SDK adapter built with no transport) sends requests with no DNS check - the gateway always supplies one, but the safety is not enforced by the type. Finally, parseImageUrl() (routes/inference.ts) is text-only with no DNS resolution; I found no local download of image URLs (they are forwarded to the provider), so this is not a live gateway SSRF, but it is a weaker check than the transport's and a future adapter that downloads images would inherit that gap. Net: strong against literal private endpoints, DNS names that currently resolve private, redirects, header injection and path escape; not a guarantee against an attacker-controlled DNS name or loopback, which is exactly the 'provider-supplied endpoint' case in the threat.

threat: A crafted backup envelope makes key derivation consume unbounded CPU and stalls the gateway event loop.
strengths: The precise unbounded-CPU vector is closed in Kernel/API/src/core/backup.ts: boundedKdf() runs before any scryptSync and rejects envelope-supplied KDF parameters unless N/r/p are safe integers >= 1, N is a power of two in [2, 65536], r <= 32, p <= 16 and 128*N*r <= 64 MiB; scryptSync is additionally passed maxmem: 64 MiB. This matters because maxmem bounds 128*N*r but not p, and p is the cheap way for a tiny envelope to multiply CPU. Validation is ordered so format/version/cipher/kdf.name/field-type checks and the 20 MiB MAX_ENVELOPE_CHARS payload cap all precede the KDF (backup.ts L73-87), while the HTTP layer caps the request body at 25 MiB by both content-length and streamed byte count (routes/backup.ts L5, core/http.ts L53-65). The bound is centralized in decryptBackup, so all three callers - export read-back (service.ts L3158), verify (L3169) and import (L3264) - are covered with no unguarded path. A named regression test (test/backup.test.js L109-124) feeds p=1e8, p=-1, N=1<<20, N=3, r=1<<20, p=1.5 and a string p, asserts each is refused with /KDF parameters/ before scrypt work, and confirms genuine defaults still round-trip; the suite passes 7/7. /v1/backup is in the management prefix list (server.ts L406), so with key enforcement on an unauthenticated caller is rejected (test/admin-gate.test.js). The fix is committed (e4ad081b 'Fix four security-audit findings', 2026-11-20) and is present in the live dist build and the published CLI gateway bundle (cli/server/gateway.mjs).
weaknesses: The mitigation bounds per-envelope cost but does not remove the event-loop stall named in the threat: decryption still uses synchronous scryptSync, so even an accepted envelope at the top of the allowed range (N=16384, r=8, p=16) measured ~856 ms of blocking CPU on this machine; there is no worker-thread/async handoff or wall-clock budget, only parameter proxies. There is also no request-rate limit on this surface: the RateLimiter in core/rate-limit.ts is applied only to public LLM routes (server.ts L234-237, isPublicLlmRoute), not to /v1/backup/verify or /import, so an authorized caller - or any local process when key enforcement is off, the documented local mode - can replay expensive-but-bounded envelopes and keep the loop busy. The scryptSync call sits outside decryptBackup's try/catch (backup.ts L82-87 vs L88), so parameter sets that pass the application bound but exceed OpenSSL's own maxmem - e.g. N=65536/r=8/p=16 or N=16384/r=32/p=16, both allowed by 128*N*r <= 64 MiB - throw 'Invalid scrypt params', which escapes as a generic bad request; a fast failure rather than a stall, but an untested edge. The regression test probes a handful of hostile values rather than the accepted boundaries (p=16, N=65536, r=32 are not asserted as accepted), and the passphrase has a minimum but no maximum length (only the 25 MiB body cap contains it). Finally, the packaged desktop artifacts under release/ (app.asar and app.asar.unpacked/.../core/backup.js, built 2026-11-12) predate the 2026-11-20 fix and still carry unbounded scryptSync, so an operator running those binaries rather than the source/dist or the npm CLI bundle is unprotected until they are rebuilt.

threat: A prompt-influenced model escapes an operator-approved local-tool root via a symlink and reads outside files.
strengths: A dedicated executor (Kernel/API/src/core/local-tool-executor.ts) enforces realpath containment on both the caller-supplied path (resolveInside/chooseRoot) and every file produced by directory enumeration (containedInRoots), which is exactly the symlink-inside-an-approved-root escape path. local_read realpaths and then reads the canonical path; local_grep skips enumerated entries whose realpath lands outside every approved root. Commit e4ad081b fixed audit finding 4 (medium) with a regression test that plants a symlink to an outside secret and asserts the marker is absent; all five executor tests pass locally and the built dist contains the fix. The surface is opt-in (OMNIHILBRAS_LOCAL_TOOLS=1 AND absolute OMNIHILBRAS_LOCAL_TOOL_ROOTS), exposes only read/glob/grep with no shell, write or network capability, caps output at 64 KiB, and is bounded to four tool rounds; build-time guards assert the realpath usage and absence of process/write/network APIs, and the SPEC states the realpath guarantee.
weaknesses: Check-then-use TOCTOU remains in local_grep: containedInRoots() calls realpathSync on a file but the following readFileSync(file) reads the original, possibly symlinked path, so an actor able to swap the link in that window could still escape — not reachable by the read-only model itself, but weaker than O_NOFOLLOW/openat. The revalidation is applied at the grep read site rather than inside walk(), so a future tool that reads walked files could silently reintroduce the bug; local_glob does not re-realpath enumerated entries (only names are returned today, so no content leak, but symlink metadata is exposed). Hardlinks are indistinguishable to realpath (not a model capability here). The secondary local-tool-root surface, the OpenCode bridge, delegates path enforcement to upstream OpenCode: 'project' mode denies external_directory but has no repo-level symlink regression test, and the default mode deliberately allows reads anywhere the gateway user can, so an operator-approved root is not the default posture there. Generic fs errors are returned to the model via error.message and may echo absolute host paths.

threat: A credential reaches browser storage, a log, or version control.
strengths: All three surfaces are guarded by asserted mechanisms rather than prose, and the guards pass on the current tree. BROWSER STORAGE: tests/browser-storage.test.js allows exactly four non-credential localStorage keys (sidebar collapse, theme, reduce-motion, skipped update version), names credential-shaped identifiers by splitting camelCase (so apiKey/refreshToken/userToken are caught where a \bkey\b regex would not), resolves string-constant and template-literal keys, rejects credential-shaped values, asserts sessionStorage, document.cookie writes, IndexedDB and the Cache API at zero, and pins the access count at 12 — all 6 subtests pass. Only the four benign keys exist in src/ (dashboard.tsx, SettingsPage.tsx, ThemeToggle.tsx, DashboardShell.tsx, useUpdateState.ts). The dashboard tells users to copy their own session token from a third-party site's storage (src/lib/webSessionProviders.ts) but never writes it itself. VERSION CONTROL: tests/no-secrets.test.js scans all 1519 tracked files (via git ls-files) for 15 vendor credential shapes (gateway ohk_, npm, GitHub, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, AWS, Google, Slack, Discord, private-key blocks, JWT, bearer values), with empty exemptions asserted, pattern liveness proven by assembled samples, content-based binary skipping, and self-flagging assertions — all 7 subtests pass. .gitignore explicitly ignores .env.*, connections.json, secrets.enc.json, secrets.key, api-keys.json, usage.json, dashboard-token and .omnihilbras/, and only .env.example is tracked. LOGS AND RESPONSES: Kernel/API/src/core/provider-error.ts toJSON() deliberately drops details and cause because provider payloads may carry credentials/prompt data; Kernel/API/src/core/usage-store.ts has a FORBIDDEN_RECORD_FIELDS denylist (content, message, prompt, response, body, headers, apiKey, authorization, system) enforced by Kernel/API/test/usage-store.test.js including hand-edited-file injection; Kernel/API/src/routes/logs.ts streams only those sanitized usage records behind the management gate (Kernel/API/test/log-stream-route.test.js). Kernel/API/test/credential-projection.test.js asserts tunnel tokens are never returned (hasToken only), proxy-pool credentials are redacted on read (***:***) and refusals never quote the credential value. API keys are random, SHA-256 hashed, revealed once and compared in constant time (core/api-keys.ts, core/api-key-manager.ts, tests). Credentials at rest use secure-store.ts atomicWrite: 0700 directory, 0600 file, chmod after rename, fsync, symlink refusal. Backups are AES-256-GCM with scrypt and an unstored passphrase (core/backup.ts).
weaknesses: No generic guard scans source for credential-valued log statements: a new console.log(apiKey) would not fail any test. sign-in-coordinator.ts:48 deliberately console.error's a ProviderError cause.message, and providerSaid() (core/oauth.ts) folds provider-controlled response-body text into public sign-in error strings rendered in the callback page — a provider that echoed a credential into an error body would put it in a log and the UI. The no-secrets scanner reads only git ls-files by design (its threat is version control), so untracked credentials are invisible to it; the working tree currently holds .env.local with a Vercel OIDC JWT (gitignored, apparently expired), showing a credential can sit in the repo directory until force-added. The browser-storage test walks only .ts/.tsx under src/, so browser-facing code added under site/, cli/server-src/ or desktop/ would not be covered. The 15 scanner patterns cover known vendor key shapes; a novel internal secret format or a base64/hex-re-encoded credential would not match. A key that reached history requires rotation, which no test automates. On balance the asserted controls cover the realistic paths well; the residuals are coverage-boundary and provider-trust gaps rather than a live leak.

threat: A stale or recycled recorded PID causes the CLI launcher to signal an unrelated same-user process.
strengths: Both recorded-run paths gate signals on an identity check rather than liveness alone. The checkout launcher (bin/omnihilbras.js) records process groups in run.json (gatewayGroup/dashboardGroup, not bare pids, because pnpm's child binds the port), requires groupIsOurs(pgid) before every stopPreviousRun() signal, rejects non-integer/<=1 ids, and matches live /proc members' command lines against omnihilbras/vite; ports are confirmed held by our own previous run BEFORE anything is stopped, so a port typo cannot cost a running server, and signalGroup() targets -pgid. The published bundled path is stronger: cli/lib/bundled-state.mjs's stopBundledServers() filters to safe positive pids, checks liveness, then requires a server-specific command-line match (/gateway\.mjs|static\.mjs/) and leaves foreign/reused pids alone (refusals reported, record retained) unless --force is explicit. That one helper is now shared by the stop and restart verbs and, since e4ad081b (security audit 2026-11-20, finding 2), by the bare launcher's stopRecorded(), closing the previously unguarded SIGTERM-on-start. Command-line lookup is cross-platform there (/proc, WMI on Windows, ps on macOS). Records are 0600 in a 0700 XDG state dir; a generation counter prevents stale child-close events from respawning duplicates. tests/cli-lifecycle.test.js drives the stop decision with injected alive/commandLine/kill and proves a reused foreign pid is refused and never signalled; tests/launcher.test.js pins the group-ownership gate and the port-check-before-stop ordering. The repo also knows how to do two-factor process identification when it matters (Kernel/API/src/core/opencode-runtime.ts requires both cmdline markers AND our XDG state home in /proc/<pid>/environ).
weaknesses: The checkout launcher still degrades to exactly the naive check this threat describes: groupIsOurs() returns pidIsAlive(pgid) (a bare process.kill(pid,0)) whenever processGroupMembers() finds no members — always on macOS/Windows (no /proc) and on Linux when a group has dissolved but its numeric id is now a live unrelated same-user PID — and signalGroup() then falls back from kill(-pgid) to kill(pgid), which would signal that unrelated process. Its positive check is a loose substring ('omnihilbras' or 'vite'), the same shape the file's own header condemns in the reference launcher (editor/grep/str); another project's Vite server or a shell/grep whose argv contains the word qualifies, and members.some() means one matching member vouches for the whole group. Neither record uses its stored startedAt to bind the process start time (e.g. /proc stat field 22), so PID recycling is not actually detected beyond command-line coincidence, and check-then-kill is TOCTOU. tests/launcher.test.js is source-text assertion only and never exercises a real recycled pid or group, and the bundled decision tests inject commandLine() so the real /proc/WMI/ps readers are untested. cli/server-src/main.mjs clearPort() (adjacent but same-user process safety) kills a port holder without --force whenever its command matches the broad /node|vite|pnpm|omnihilbras|next-server/i regex. Finally the two schemes (run.json groups vs bundled.json pids) coexist with different identity rules, a drift surface even though both currently check something. Net: the confirmed audit gap is fixed and the common path is solid; the residuals are the Linux-empty-group/non-Linux liveness fallbacks, loose markers and no start-time binding.
